## Time and Tsibbles

The U.S. retail sales data come from FRED and contain monthly seasonally adjusted (RSAFS) and non-seasonally adjusted (RSAFSNA) retail and food-services sales, measured in millions of dollars. In `retail_ts`, `Month` is the monthly index and `series_id` is the key. The `can_gas` data come from the `canadian_gas` dataset distributed with `fpp3`; Canadian natural gas production is recorded monthly from January 1960 through February 2005 in billions of cubic meters. `can_gas` uses `Month` as an index and has no key because there is one time series.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)

retail_raw_guess <- read_csv("data/retail_sales_raw.csv")
head(retail_raw_guess)

retail_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/retail_sales_raw.csv", na = ".",
  col_types = cols(observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
                   RSAFS = col_double(), RSAFSNA = col_double())
)
head(retail_raw)
```

**2.2a:** R identified `observation_date` as a date variable (`<date>`) and the two sales series as numeric variables (`<dbl>`). The dates were also specified explicitly when re-reading the CSV so R would not need to guess column types.

```{r}
retail_raw_long <- retail_raw |>
  select(observation_date, RSAFS, RSAFSNA) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(RSAFS, RSAFSNA),
               names_to = "series_id", values_to = "sales")
head(retail_raw_long)

retail_ts <- retail_raw_long |>
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(observation_date)) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month, key = series_id)
head(retail_ts)
has_gaps(retail_ts)

head(canadian_gas)
key_vars(canadian_gas)
index_var(canadian_gas)
can_gas <- canadian_gas |> select(Month, Volume)
head(can_gas)
has_gaps(can_gas)
```

**2.4 and 2.5:** `retail_ts` uses `Month` as its index and `series_id` as its key, with monthly frequency `[1M]`. `can_gas` has `Month` as its index and no key. Missing-month checks are shown above; the number of series with gaps is `r sum(as_tibble(has_gaps(retail_ts))$.gaps, na.rm = TRUE)` for retail and `r sum(as_tibble(has_gaps(can_gas))$.gaps, na.rm = TRUE)` for Canadian gas.

```{r}
can_gas_recent <- can_gas |> filter(Month >= yearmonth("1990 Jan"))
head(can_gas_recent)

can_gas_recent <- can_gas_recent |>
  mutate(year = year(Month),
         month = month(Month, label = TRUE),
         quarter = quarter(Month))
month_avgs <- can_gas_recent |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarize(avg_volume = mean(Volume), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(month_avgs, digits = 3)

can_gas_recent |>
  mutate(next_month = Month + 1,
         same_month_last_year = Month - 12) |>
  head()

can_gas_q <- can_gas |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2004 Dec")) |>
  index_by(Quarter = yearquarter(Month)) |>
  summarize(Volume = sum(Volume))
head(can_gas_q)
can_gas_q |> autoplot(Volume) +
  labs(title = "Canadian Gas Production — Quarterly Totals",
       y = "Billions of cubic meters per quarter") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**2.6b:** For Canadian gas production from January 1990 onward, **December** has the highest mean monthly volume (17.148 billion cubic meters), while **June** has the lowest (14.945 billion cubic meters).

**2.6d:** Quarterly production should use sums because monthly production is a flow measured over each month, so the quarter's total includes all three months. Aggregating to quarters smooths some within-quarter changes, but a recurring seasonal pattern is still visible at the quarterly frequency.

```{r}
retail_ts |> autoplot(sales)

retail_ts |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(title = "U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales",
       subtitle = "Seasonally adjusted vs. not seasonally adjusted",
       x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

can_gas |>
  autoplot(Volume) +
  labs(title = "Canadian Natural Gas Production", x = NULL,
       y = "Billions of cubic meters") +
  theme_minimal()

can_gas |>
  autoplot(Volume) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Canadian Gas Production — Formatted Axis", x = NULL,
       y = "Billions of cubic meters") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**2.7b:** The non-seasonally-adjusted retail sales series has repeated within-year increases and decreases, including a holiday-related sales peak and a subsequent decline. The seasonally adjusted version substantially reduces these predictable seasonal swings, but the two series share their broad long-run upward trend and major economy-wide changes.

**2.7d:** I added `scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma())` to format the y-axis values more clearly.

## Transformations

**3.1a:** In the level graph, the seasonal variation is not the same size in every decade. The fluctuations generally become larger as production initially grows, but the relationship is not uniform across the whole sample.

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |> mutate(log_volume = log(Volume))
can_gas |>
  autoplot(log_volume) +
  labs(title = "Log Canadian Gas Production", y = "log(Volume)") +
  theme_minimal()

retail_nsa <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  mutate(log_sales = log(sales))
retail_nsa |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(title = "NSA Retail Sales — Level", y = "Millions of dollars") +
  theme_minimal()
retail_nsa |>
  autoplot(log_sales) +
  labs(title = "NSA Retail Sales — Log", y = "log(sales)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**3.1b:** Logging Canadian gas production compresses large values and makes proportional changes more comparable over time. It makes the early growth look more nearly linear and makes the seasonal swings more even in scale, although it does not remove seasonality or the changing trend. Therefore the log transformation is useful, but it is not a complete model of the data.

**3.1c:** The case for taking logs is particularly clear for retail sales, where the overall level rises substantially and seasonal swings in dollars tend to grow with the level. The log graph represents percentage changes more consistently across the sample.

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(growth_direct = 100 * difference(Volume) / lag(Volume),
         growth_logdiff = 100 * difference(log_volume),
         growth_gap = abs(growth_direct - growth_logdiff))
can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_direct) +
  labs(title = "Exact Monthly Canadian Gas Growth", y = "Growth (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_gap) +
  labs(title = "Difference: Exact vs Log Growth", y = "Percentage points") +
  theme_minimal()

retail_ts <- retail_ts |>
  group_by_key() |>
  mutate(growth_mom = 100 * difference(log(sales))) |>
  ungroup()
retail_ts |>
  autoplot(growth_mom) +
  labs(title = "Month-over-Month Growth: SA vs. NSA Retail Sales",
       x = NULL, y = "Growth rate (%)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**3.2a:** The median absolute difference between the exact and log-difference monthly growth rates is `r round(median(can_gas$growth_gap, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` percentage points, while the largest is `r round(max(can_gas$growth_gap, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` percentage points. The approximation is generally close, but the difference is larger when the monthly percentage change itself is large.

**3.3:** Non-seasonally-adjusted retail sales growth is noisier than adjusted growth because it includes regular within-year sales movements. The adjusted series removes much of that predictable seasonal movement and makes unusual month-to-month changes easier to recognize. This agrees with the comparison of the levels in Part 2.7b.

## Seasonality

```{r}
retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in NSA Retail Sales",
       y = "Millions of dollars") +
  theme_minimal()

retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in SA Retail Sales",
       y = "Millions of dollars") +
  theme_minimal()

can_gas |>
  gg_season(log_volume) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Pattern in Log Canadian Gas Production",
       y = "log(Volume)") +
  theme_minimal()

can_gas |>
  gg_subseries(log_volume) +
  labs(title = "Subseries Plot: Canadian Gas Production",
       y = "log(Volume)")
```

```{r}
gas_month_means <- can_gas |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(month = month(Month, label = TRUE)) |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarise(mean_log = mean(log_volume), .groups = "drop")
```

**4.1b:** In the NSA seasonal plot, years have recognizable recurring peaks and dips by month. The SA plot has a much weaker repeating monthly pattern, which is what seasonal adjustment is designed to achieve.

**4.1c:** Canadian gas production shows a repeating annual cycle. Based on the full-sample log-volume monthly averages, production is highest in **`r as.character(gas_month_means$month[which.max(gas_month_means$mean_log)])`** and lowest in **`r as.character(gas_month_means$month[which.min(gas_month_means$mean_log)])`**. The cycle is consistent with seasonal changes in heating-related gas demand.

**4.2:** The subseries plot separates the history of each calendar month and marks the average for that month. The differences among these monthly averages confirm seasonality while the individual month histories reveal the trend over time.

```{r}
retail_nsa_x13 <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  model(x13 = X_13ARIMA_SEATS(sales)) |>
  components()
retail_nsa_x13 |> autoplot()

sa_compare <- retail_nsa_x13 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Month, mine = season_adjust) |>
  left_join(
    retail_ts |>
      filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
      as_tibble() |>
      transmute(Month, census = sales),
    by = "Month"
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (log(mine) - log(census)))
sa_compare |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = pct_diff)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "My X-13 Seasonal Adjustment Minus the Census Bureau's",
       x = NULL, y = "Difference (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
season_month <- retail_nsa_x13 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(month = month(Month, label = TRUE), factor = sales / season_adjust) |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarise(mean_factor = mean(factor, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
largest_adjustment_month <- season_month |> slice_max(mean_factor, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
comparison_max <- sa_compare |> filter(is.finite(pct_diff)) |>
  slice_max(abs(pct_diff), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
```

**4.3a:** The seasonal factor is highest in **`r as.character(largest_adjustment_month$month)`**, with the typical factor implying about **`r round(100 * (largest_adjustment_month$mean_factor - 1), 1)`%** higher sales than the seasonally adjusted level. The raw seasonal swings get larger in dollar terms as sales grow, consistent with the multiplicative seasonal decomposition.

**4.3b:** The mean absolute log-percentage difference between my adjustment and the official Census adjustment is **`r round(mean(abs(sa_compare$pct_diff), na.rm = TRUE), 3)` percentage points**. The largest absolute difference is **`r round(abs(comparison_max$pct_diff), 3)` percentage points** in **`r as.character(comparison_max$Month)`**. A small but nonzero difference is expected because Census uses tailored settings, category-specific adjustment, and calendar/outlier treatment rather than the default X-13 options.

```{r}
can_gas_fit <- can_gas |>
  model(TSLM(log_volume ~ trend() + season()))
report(can_gas_fit)
can_gas_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = log_volume, color = "Actual")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted, color = "Fitted")) +
  labs(title = "Linear Trend + Seasonal Dummies Fit: Canadian Gas Production",
       y = "log(Volume)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

can_gas_fit |> gg_tsresiduals()
can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

```{r}
model_coefs <- tidy(can_gas_fit)
trend_coefficient <- model_coefs |> filter(grepl("trend", term)) |> slice(1)
strongest_season <- model_coefs |>
  filter(grepl("season", term)) |>
  slice_max(abs(statistic), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
ljung_result <- can_gas_fit |> augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24)
```

**4.4a:** The estimated trend coefficient is 0.003973, implying approximately **0.397% average monthly growth** in Canadian gas production. The sixth-month (June) seasonal dummy has the largest absolute t-statistic (**4.777**); its coefficient is about -0.2512 relative to the omitted January category, consistent with lower midyear production.

**4.4b:** The fitted values capture the broad upward trend and the regular month-of-year seasonal pattern. However, the straight-line trend misses longer movements, particularly the rapid changes in the earlier decades and the flatter or changing trend in later decades. That leaves runs of residuals above or below zero instead of purely random deviations.

**4.4c:** Residuals exhibit long persistent runs and substantial positive autocorrelation in the ACF, so they are not white noise. The Ljung–Box statistic at 24 lags is **7,774.218**, with a p-value reported as essentially zero (below 0.001). We reject the null of no autocorrelation at the 5% level, suggesting the model misses predictable dynamics beyond a linear trend and fixed seasonality.

## Forecast Evaluation

```{r}
gas_cv_fc <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)
acc_exp <- gas_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE))
knitr::kable(acc_exp, digits = 3)
```

**5.1a:** The first evaluated one-month-ahead forecast is **January 1980** and the last is **February 2005** (March 2005 has no actual value available for scoring). With an expanding window, seasonal naïve has **MAE 0.562** and **RMSE 0.702**, while trend-plus-season TSLM has **MAE 4.009** and **RMSE 4.362**. Both measures agree that seasonal naïve forecasts more accurately.

```{r}
errs <- gas_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(can_gas) |> select(Month, actual = Volume),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e) |>
  na.omit()
dm_result <- forecast::dm.test(errs$snaive, errs$tslm, h = 1, power = 1)
dm_result
```

**5.2a:** The Diebold–Mariano test with one-step-ahead forecasts and absolute-error loss gives **DM = -31.278** and **p < 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶**. Therefore, at the 5% level, I reject the null hypothesis of equal expected forecast accuracy. The smaller MAE of seasonal naïve indicates it is the more accurate of these two models over the expanding-window evaluation period.

```{r}
gas_roll_fc <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  slide_tsibble(.size = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)
acc_roll <- gas_roll_fc |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE))
knitr::kable(acc_roll, digits = 3)
```

**5.3a:** With the rolling 240-month window, seasonal naïve has **MAE 0.562** and **RMSE 0.702**, while TSLM has **MAE 2.095** and **RMSE 2.425**. Compared with the expanding window, seasonal naïve is unchanged, while TSLM improves noticeably (MAE falls from 4.009 to 2.095, and RMSE from 4.362 to 2.425). The seasonal naïve forecast uses the previous year’s corresponding month regardless of window length; TSLM instead reestimates a linear trend, so restricting it to more recent history helps it adapt to trend changes visible in Part 4.4b. The seasonal naïve model still has smaller errors.

## Reflection

The residual graph from the linear trend and seasonal dummy model shows long periods of positive and negative errors rather than random fluctuations around zero. The ACF and Ljung–Box test suggest that there is still substantial autocorrelation to explain. Even though the regression accounts for regular seasonality, it is too rigid to capture shifts in the underlying path of gas production. In the expanding-window forecasting comparison, **`r acc_exp$.model[which.min(acc_exp$MAE)]`** achieved the lower MAE, showing that the simpler model may forecast better than the fitted trend model. A future model could allow for changing trends and autocorrelated disturbances, rather than assuming one fixed straight-line trend explains the whole sample.
